messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

Amir presents as a man carrying an invisible, immense weight. At 40, his posture is perpetually braced, his shoulders tight beneath the soft fabric of his polo shirt. He is a senior software engineer, a man whose career is built on logic, order, and predictable systems. He speaks of his life before last year with a quiet nostalgia, as if describing a different person. That person, he explains, was lighter. He smiled more. He didn't check the structural engineering reports for every building his children entered.

The shift occurred eighteen months ago, during a family trip to his hometown. It was the first time he had taken his wife, Layla, and their two young children to see the house where he grew up. The trip was meant to be a celebration, a connection to his roots. For two weeks, it was exactly that. He remembers the smell of his aunt's cooking, the sound of his children playing with their cousins in the courtyard, the familiar comfort of his childhood bedroom.

He was on the second floor, helping his uncle fix a leaky faucet, when the world dissolved into noise. It wasn't a shake at first, he recalls, but a deep, violent roar from the earth itself. The feeling was not of the ground moving side to side, but of it simply ceasing to exist. He remembers a single, lucid thought-Layla, the kids-before the floor gave way.

He woke up in darkness, pinned by a concrete beam. The air was thick with a chalky dust that burned his throat. For hours, all he knew was the crushing weight on his legs, the muffled screams that eventually faded, and the terrifying, rhythmic dripping of water somewhere nearby. When the rescuers finally pulled him out into the blinding daylight, the familiar street was gone, replaced by a landscape of rubble. His wife and children had been in the courtyard and were miraculously safe, but his aunt and uncle, who were in the kitchen below him, were gone.

Since returning to the United States, Amir has tried to reconstruct the architecture of his old life, but the foundation is cracked. At work, he finds it nearly impossible to concentrate. The complex lines of code he once navigated with ease now blur into meaningless symbols. His mind, once a precise instrument for problem-solving, is now a chaotic loop of intrusive images: the splintering of wood, the specific shade of gray of the concrete dust, the look on his wife's face when she saw him being carried from the wreckage. He works exclusively from home now, unable to bear the thought of being in a high-rise office tower.

At home, he is a ghost. Layla describes him as being "behind glass." He is physically present but emotionally inaccessible. He no longer initiates games with his children, and when they climb on him, he flinches, an involuntary recoil from the memory of the weight. Any sudden, low rumble-a passing garbage truck, the hum of the furnace kicking on-sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. He will stop mid-sentence, his eyes wide, his body rigid, waiting for the floor to drop out from under him again.

Sleep offers no escape. He is plagued by nightmares of being trapped, of the darkness and the dust. He often wakes up gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs, convinced the ceiling is about to collapse. He spends his nights sitting in the living room, watching the news on mute, feeling a strange, hollow guilt. He, the logical engineer, built a life on the assumption of solid ground. Now, he lives with the constant, terrifying awareness that at any moment, everything can simply fall apart.
